profile.Aims of the course:
Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) can be defined as "Non-trivial process of identifying valid, novel, potentially useful and ultimately understandable patterns from data". This modern branch of computer science is on the edge of database technologies, statistics and artificial intelligence. KDD techniques can be used to solve classification, prediction, summarization or segmentation
tasks on various application areas.
Students will get familiar with the methods used for knowledge discovery in 
databases from both theoretical and practical point of view. The main focus of the lectures will be on description of used data mining methods and algorithms. In practical part, the students will work with selected data mining systems.
profile.Learning outcomes and competences:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
  - understand the role of KDD for data analysis,
  - understand the basic principles of various data mining algorithms,
  - understand the basic methods of evaluation of created models,
  - understand basic preprocessing operations,
  - formulate and solve KDD tasks for real-world data,
  - use selected data mining systems.
profile.Course contents:
- The process of KDD: tasks, methodologies, tools
 - The background for KDD: databases, statistics, machine learning
 - Machine learning methods: decision trees, decision rules, association 
   rules, neural nets, bayesian methods, instance based  
   learning 
 - Evaluation what has been learned
 - Data preprocessing methods
 - Text mining
 - Real-world applications

profile.Aims of the course: The aim of the course is to explain basic types of financial derivatives, mechanics of their markets, their application for hedging and/or speculation, and their valuation. We will introduce basic modelling techniques for stock prices, exchange rates, and other underlying assets. These models will be used for valuation of plain derivatives (forwards, futures, options, and swaps) in an arbitrage-less market. Some specialized derivatives like exotic options, credit, weather, energy, and other derivatives will be also briefly introduced. Practical issues of derivatives trading, valuation, and risk management will be discussed as well.
profile.Course contents:
1. Introduction - principles of financial derivatives (Exchange-traded and over the counter markets, forward, option and future contracts, hedging versus speculation, advantages and disadvantages of derivatives over on-balance sheet products, accounting issues)
2. Mechanics of futures trading and their application (specification of a futures contract, daily settlement and margin, delivery, quoting conventions, relationship between spot and futures price, forwards versus futures, hedging with futures)
3. Determination of forward and futures prices (the cost of carry, valuing forward contracts, forward versus futures prices, futures prices on stock indices, currencies, and commodities, contango and backwardation)
4. Interest rate and currency swaps (types of rates, day count issues, zero-coupon rates and cash-flow discounting, forward rates and forward rate agreements, Eurodollar and Treasury Bond futures, plain vanilla interest rate and cross-currency swaps, valuation, credit risk, ISDA agreement)
5. Mechanics of options markets (types of options, underlying assets, quoting and properties of stock options, exchange traded versus OTC options, put-call parity, trading strategies, warrants)
6. Modeling of underlying prices and options valuation (binomial trees, risk-neutral valuation, continuous time stochastic processes, the process for a stock price, concepts underlying the Black-Scholes pricing formula, implied versus quoted volatility)
7. Options on stock indices, currencies, and futures (option pricing formula for the different types of options, the Greek letters, Delta, Theta, Gamma etc., Delta hedging, volatility smiles)
8. Introduction to exotic, credit, weather, energy, and insurance derivatives (barrier, binary, Asian etc. options, basic types of credit, weather, energy, any insurance derivatives)

profile.Aims of the course: The aim is to get students acquainted with the basic concepts of risk management in both financial and non-financial companies.  After graduation of the course the students should be able expertly communicate with specialist in RM.
profile.Learning outcomes and competences:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
- manage advanced methods of risk management and communicate with specialists relating especially to market risk, interest rate risk and credit risk.
profile.Course contents:
1.Classification of  financial risks.
2.Theoretical background (von Neuman-Morgenstern utility function, risk premium, subjective probabilities, measures of risk).
3.Market risk, CAPM, beta and alpha of asset, systematic and unsystematic risk, arbitrage model, factor risks, simple and sophisticate diversification.
4.Interest rate risk. 
5.Duration and convexity.
6.Immunization of interest rate portfolio.
7.FRA, interest rate futures.
8.Interest rate swap and its applications. 
9.Interest rate options (cap, floor, collar).
10.Characterization of yield curve  (level, slope, curvature), Nelson-Siegel 
   parametrization.
11.Credit risk, classical methods of credit risk management.
12.Scoring models.
13.Portfolio approach to credit risk management.
14.Expected and unexpected loss, portfolio approach to credit risk.
15.Trading credit risk, credit derivatives (syndication, securitization, credit derivatives, CDO).

profile.Aims of the course:
Basic knowledge of neurophysiology and neuropsychology will be discussed with regard to the cognitive-computational orientation of participating students.
A) Students will be confronted to principal directions and trends in neurosciences with a particular impact on cognitive framework
B) Basic literature and relevant information sources will be submitted and critical lecture and discussions initiated
C) Background issues in the domains of neuro-informatics, neuro-economics and neuro-politics will be presented and discussed
profile.Learning outcomes and competences: Upon successful completion of this course, students will become oriented in the relationship between brain structure and its function, with a particular impact on emotions, planning, decision making and reward and selection principles. They will be able to understand and critically comment contemporary literature. The essay will place the acquired knowledge into a large context and verify the understanding of basic items and their relationships.
profile.Course contents:
1) Cell membrane – structure and function (principles of transmembrane potentials and conduction, action potentials, myelin and its role, alterations of signal processing – epileptic discharges)
2) Ionic channels and pumps (voltage gated channels, mechanisms of blocking and inactivation, restitution of resting potential – ionic pumps)
3) Synaptic transmission – (synaptic structure, principal neurotransmitters; the role of calcium in synaptic transmission – second messengers and related modifications in function and shape of neurons and dendrites)
4) Pain and sensibility; (tactile perception and conduction, signal modulation at different levels from the spinal cord to the thalamus, cortical integration – modules, pain modulation, phantom pain)
5) Movements (different aspects of motor functions – principles of regulation, the passage from initiation to realization of a movement, modulation of an ongoing movement – the role of the cerebellum)
6) Brain development, formation of neuronal connections; synaptic and neuronal plasticity (critical periods, growth factors, signal proteins, synaptic plasticity, long term potentiation and learning)
7) Cognition – general aspects, language and communication (primary and secondary brain areas, associative cortex, language and its localization)
8) Memory and amnesia (different subtypes of memory, the key role of hippocampus in declarative memory, procedural memory, amnesias, mechanisms of learning, the aging brain)
9) Lateralization, emotions, visual perception (the dominant and non-dominant hemispheres, visuo-spatial perception, emotions and the limbic system, amygdala emotional behavior)
10) Vigilance and consciousness, awakeness and sleep (brain stem functions, attention, subconsciousness, circadian rythmes, sleep stages and pathology)
11) Frontal functions, the social brain (planning and decision making, voluntary acting, social behavior, personality, intelligence)
12) Interaction between the nervous system and other systems (immunity, hormones, homeostasis) (feedback circuits, integrity of the organism and physiological interactions, brain and sexuality)
13) Introduction to neuro-economics (behavior and decision making under economical aspects, marketing and neurobiology of emotions)

profile.Aims of the course:
The course aims to provide students with the opportunity to reinforce and further develop key interpersonal skills essential for the successful implementation of proposed solutions, effective teamwork, and leadership. Connecting students' professional knowledge with the development of soft skills prepares them for the complex demands of contemporary practice.
Throughout the course, students will draw on theoretical knowledge and case studies as well as their own team-developed solutions. This practical approach allows them to master advanced techniques in communication, presentation, and change management in dynamic environments. Emphasis is placed on design and creative thinking methodologies, which systematically develop soft skills and are supported by modern technologies.
Each core area of the course is strategically chosen to cultivate skills that enable students to manage complex projects and challenges. The course content focuses on the implementation of evidence-based solutions and strategic communication, including storytelling. The course output (a proposal presentation) simulates a real-world work environment, helping students prepare for professional challenges. This course leads to the follow-up course Meta-Skills for Practice – Hackathon.
profile.Learning outcomes and competences:
- Building on the Problem-Solving course from the bachelor's program, students will deepen their comprehensive approach to problem solving, from identification to strategic communication with all stakeholders.
- Students will acquire the basic concept of the implementation of evidence-based solutions, a key skill in defending proposals to experts and laypersons alike.
- Students will gain insight into the principles of strategic communication in the context of solution implementation.
- Students will reinforce and further develop teamwork skills, emphasizing teamwork and self-reflection as a catalyst for improvement. They will learn skills to build trust, foster collaboration through team or organizational communication, assertive communication, and persuasion.
- Students will improve their critical thinking, creativity, time management, and resilience to failure by addressing real-world problems, better preparing them for professional life.
- Students will strengthen and expand their skills in using artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to solve problems and implement solutions in practice.
- Practical tools and modern technologies used in the course: Students will use tools such as Google LM Notebook (for project collaboration and analysis), Canva (for idea visualization and storytelling), and Kahoot! (for interactive learning and feedback) to develop their skills.
- Students will strengthen and refine their presentation skills to defend proposed solutions in both Czech and English.
profile.Course contents:
• Introduction to the course: Overview of the content, requirements, and technologies used. Assignment of the semester-long team project.
• Evidence-Based Implementation: Concept and main principles of transferring theoretical knowledge into practice and justifying implementation decisions with evidence.
• Manual for Evidence-Based Implementation: Creating structured guides for solution implementation.
• Evidence Search and Critical Evaluation: Understanding and utilizing the evidence pyramid.
• Strategic Communication with Target Groups and Stakeholders: Principles and concepts of strategic communication tailored to key stakeholders.
• Steps to Create a Strategic Communication Plan: Setting goals and identifying target groups, crafting key messages, choosing communication channels, developing timelines, and incorporating reflection.
• Storytelling: Creating compelling narratives to effectively present complex ideas. Principles of memorability and emotional connection with target groups.
• Creating concrete examples of "story communication“.
• Presentation of the team proposal for solution implementation: The students present their proposal for the implementation of an evidence-based solution.

profile.Aims of the course: Provide introduction to the principles and concepts of of project management in general and IS/ICT project in particular. Apprise of fundamentals and to obtain practical experience of standard project management methods (MMDIS, TOC, PMBOK, PRINCE2) and tools (MS Project).  Provide overview of further aspects of IS/ICT project management: project management procedure, projects coordination, IS/ICT organization, role and teams specification, project planning techniques and techniques, computer-aided project management tools.
profile.Learning outcomes and competences: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to prepare project, plan project, manage and control project, evaluate projects, to use projects IS/ICT planning and managing techniques and tools. Students will be able to select project management methodology and adapt methodic into specific project conditions.
profile.Course contents:
Introduction to Project Management, IS/ICT Project Management, Project Critical Success Factors.
IS/ICT strategies and IS/ICT project setting.
Formal and Informal Project Management, Organizational Structures, Organizing and Staffing the Project Office and Team, Defining the Project Manager's Role, Defining the Project Executive's Role,  Defining Project Coordinator's Role.
Team Building, Leadership in a Project Environment, Project Communications, Project Review Meetings,
Project Life Cycles, common work breakdowns of frequent categories of ICT projects, e.g. software engineering projects, Project Management Methodologies, Project Management Control and Business Procedures,  
Project Definition, Project Planning, Work Breakdown Structure, Procedural Documentation, Time Management, Time Scheduling, Estimating Activity Time, PERT, CPM Planning, TOC and Critical Chain.
 
Project Classification.
Project Management Software, Software Classification.
Risk Management, Definition of Risk, Risk Planning, Risk Analysis, Risk Handling,
Project Management Maturity Model, Project Management Methodologies (PMBOK, PRINCE2, COBIT, ISO standardy, IPMA standardy, MMDIS RIP, CMMI, Cobit, Val IT, ITIL)
Knowledge management in project environment. 
Methodology implementation and administration.
